name: John Jones
chief_complaint: Feeling tired and occasional headaches for 3 weeks
opening_statement: Hi Doctor, I've been feeling more tired than usual lately and I've had a few headaches. My wife suggested I come in to get checked out.
emotional_baseline: Slightly anxious but cooperative, concerned about missing work

rag_citations.quote: Most patients with hypertension are asymptomatic. Headache may occur, particularly with severe hypertension or hypertensive urgency.

symptoms.impact: Difficulty completing usual 30-minute walk without stopping

rag_citations.quote: Assess for symptoms that may indicate target organ damage or secondary causes of hypertension including fatigue, reduced exercise tolerance.
Postural symptoms may indicate volume depletion or autonomic dysfunction, important to assess before initiating treatment.

past_medical_history.current_status: Patient reports generally good health until recently

family_history: Father had 'high blood pressure' diagnosed in his 50s, currently on medication. Mother has type 2 diabetes. No family history of stroke or early cardiac disease.

social_history.alcohol: 2-3 standard drinks Friday/Saturday nights, occasional weekday beer
social_history.exercise: Previously walked 30 minutes 4-5 times per week, reduced recently due to fatigue
social_history.diet: Admits to high salt intake (processed foods, takeaway 2-3 times per week)
social_history.stress_levels: Moderate work stress - recent workplace restructure
social_history.sleep: 6-7 hours per night, sometimes difficulty falling asleep due to work concerns

examination_findings.general_appearance: Well-appearing male, mildly overweight, no acute distress

vital_signs.blood_pressure: 165/102 mmHg (right arm, sitting, appropriate cuff size)

cardiovascular.heart_sounds: Dual, no murmurs, no added sounds

respiratory.auscultation: Clear breath sounds bilaterally, no added sounds

neurological.fundoscopy: Recommended but not performed in initial consult

initial_recommended.test: Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) or home blood pressure monitoring
initial_recommended.rationale: Confirm diagnosis of hypertension outside office setting, exclude white coat hypertension
initial_recommended.etg_reference: eTG: Hypertension - Diagnosis requires confirmation with out-of-office measurements

initial_recommended.rationale: Assess for left ventricular hypertrophy or other cardiac abnormalities
Screen for diabetes given family history
Baseline renal function before commencing treatment
Assess for proteinuria indicating target organ damage

risk_stratification.australian_cvd_risk_calculator: To be calculated - likely moderate risk given age, BP, family history
risk_stratification.framingham_score: Not preferred - use Australian absolute CVD risk calculator

expected_diagnosis: Hypertension (new diagnosis, BP 165/102) - Stage 2 hypertension requiring pharmacological intervention

interventions: Increase physical activity to 150 minutes moderate exercise per week
expected_management.etg_reference: eTG: Hypertension - Lifestyle measures recommended for all patients

first_line_options.medication: Perindopril 2.5mg daily OR Ramipril 2.5mg daily (ACE inhibitor)
first_line_options.rationale: First-line for hypertension in non-diabetic patient <55 years
first_line_options.monitoring: Renal function and electrolytes at 1-2 weeks, then 3 months
first_line_options.etg_reference: eTG: Hypertension - ACE inhibitors first-line in younger patients

first_line_options.rationale: Alternative first-line if ACE inhibitor not tolerated
first_line_options.etg_reference: eTG: Hypertension - CCB suitable alternative first-line

counselling_points: Explain need for regular medication even when feeling well
Discuss potential side effects (dry cough with ACE-I)
Importance of monitoring BP at home
When to seek urgent review (BP >180/110, severe symptoms)

plan: Review in 1-2 weeks - check renal function and electrolytes post ACE-I initiation
Review in 4 weeks - assess BP response, side effects, lifestyle adherence
Arrange ABPM if office readings remain elevated
Discuss absolute CVD risk once investigations complete

key_points: Hypertension usually asymptomatic - symptoms not reliable indicator of control
Importance of lifestyle measures - can reduce medication needs
Home BP monitoring technique - rest 5 minutes, correct cuff size
Cardiovascular risk reduction - combined benefit of BP control and lifestyle changes

critical_errors.error: Failure to confirm diagnosis with out-of-office blood pressure measurements (ABPM or HBPM)
critical_errors.explanation: Single office reading insufficient to diagnose hypertension per Australian guidelines - risks overdiagnosis and unnecessary treatment

critical_errors.error: Starting antihypertensive medication without baseline renal function and electrolytes
critical_errors.explanation: Essential to check U&Es before ACE inhibitor/ARB to identify pre-existing renal impairment and prevent hyperkalemia

critical_errors.error: Prescribing beta-blocker (e.g., atenolol) as first-line therapy in uncomplicated hypertension
critical_errors.explanation: Beta-blockers no longer recommended as first-line unless specific indication (IHD, heart failure, arrhythmia)

critical_errors.error: Not assessing cardiovascular risk using Australian absolute CVD risk calculator
critical_errors.explanation: Risk stratification guides treatment intensity and statin consideration - mandatory part of hypertension work-up

critical_errors.error: Failing to provide lifestyle modification counselling before or alongside medication
critical_errors.explanation: Lifestyle measures are cornerstone of management, may reduce medication requirements

critical_errors.error: Not arranging timely follow-up (within 4 weeks) after initiating treatment
critical_errors.explanation: Early review necessary to assess response, side effects, and medication adherence

fracp_reviews.comments: Excellent representation of uncomplicated hypertension case suitable for AMC Clinical Exam. Appropriate difficulty grading (Easy) - single diagnosis, minimal comorbidities, straightforward management. Australian context well-integrated with eTG references, PBS restrictions, and MBS items. Critical errors appropriately severe - failure to confirm diagnosis or check renal function before ACE-I would indeed be major safety issues. Learning objectives target high-yield concepts. Minor suggestion: could add mention of 24-hour sodium excretion test for motivated patients wanting objective dietary assessment.
recommendations: Consider adding fundoscopy findings to examination section for completeness
Excellent use of Australian CVD risk calculator rather than Framingham - maintains local relevance

fracp_reviews.comments: Well-constructed case reflecting contemporary Australian hypertension management per 2023 eTG guidelines. BP level (165/102) appropriately staged as Grade 2 requiring pharmacological intervention. First-line medication choices align with current evidence (ACE-I for <55 years, CCB alternative). Correctly identifies need for ABPM/HBPM confirmation - critical for avoiding white coat hypertension misdiagnosis. Family history of hypertension adds realistic complexity without overcomplicating Easy difficulty case. The 4-6 critical errors appropriately balance common mistakes (beta-blocker misuse, missing renal check) with safety issues. RAG citations demonstrate proper eTG referencing. Case suitable for Year 11-12 medical student or AMC candidate practicing diagnostic and management skills.
recommendations: Consider this as template for other cardiovascular Easy-level cases

learning_objectives.objective: Demonstrate proper technique for blood pressure measurement and interpretation
key_points: Recognition of white coat hypertension risk

learning_objectives.objective: Apply Australian diagnostic criteria for hypertension requiring out-of-office confirmation
key_points: ABPM or HBPM required for confirmation
When to treat based on BP level and risk

learning_objectives.objective: Calculate and interpret Australian absolute cardiovascular disease risk
key_points: Use Australian CVD risk calculator (not Framingham)
Consider family history, ethnicity, social determinants

learning_objectives.objective: Select evidence-based first-line antihypertensive therapy per Australian guidelines
key_points: ACE inhibitor preferred for <55 years without diabetes
Beta-blockers NOT first-line unless specific indication

learning_objectives.objective: Order appropriate baseline investigations before initiating antihypertensive treatment
key_points: Mandatory: U&Es, creatinine, eGFR before ACE-I/ARB
Lipids, glucose, HbA1c for CVD risk

learning_objectives.objective: Counsel patients on lifestyle modifications for hypertension management
Recognize and manage potential adverse effects of ACE inhibitors
key_points: Dry cough (10-15% patients) - consider ARB switch
Acute kidney injury risk - contraindicated in bilateral RAS

learning_objectives.objective: Plan appropriate follow-up schedule and monitoring for newly diagnosed hypertension
key_points: 1-2 week review post-treatment initiation (renal function check)
4 week assessment of BP response and adherence
Annual CVD risk reassessment and complication screening
